en: There were no windows on Level B2 of the Rivermere City Archives.
Nora Bell disliked rooms without windows.

Not because she was claustrophobic. Because without windows, time became unreliable. Four in the afternoon looked exactly like nine at night. December looked exactly like June. The fluorescent tubes in the ceiling held the same flat brightness all day, filtered air whispered through the vents, and old paper, metal shelving, and dust combined into a smell so clean it was almost clinical.
Places like this made the past feel more dependable than the present.
Nora had always been suspicious of that.
She pushed a third archival box aside and glanced at the upper-right corner of her laptop screen.
She had been down here for three hours and twenty-one minutes.
And she still had not found what she had come for.

The story had begun as a straightforward investigation into the Alder Yard redevelopment. Two months earlier, Rivermere City Council had approved a $2.7-billion revitalization plan for the east side: old railway warehouses, abandoned chemical sites, and former riverfront industrial land would become residential towers, retail space, and public parkland.

Sunlight. Bicycles. Children. Cafés. Rows of glass balconies facing the river. Nothing in the renderings suggested that thirty years earlier the same ground had been contaminated by leaking storage tanks, industrial solvents, and heavy metals badly enough that even weeds had struggled to grow.
Nora wanted to know one thing.
At what point had land considered unfit for people become river-view condominiums worth more than eight hundred dollars a square foot?
Questions like that usually did not require a dead body.

She opened a 1998 land-risk assessment register. Green hard cover. Corners worn pale. This batch had not yet been scanned, so she wore the thin cotton gloves issued by the archives and turned each page by hand.
The first pages were reference numbers.
Then the company names she had been reading for hours: Halden Urban Group. Prairie Remediation Services. Northline Environmental. Mercer & Pike Legal.
Companies went bankrupt. Companies changed names. Companies were acquired. Directors died. Lawyers retired. Twenty-eight years was enough time to turn a chain of responsibility into rubble.
Nora set her phone beside the register and photographed a line of figures.
Nora stared at the name for two seconds.
Journalists developed a habit after enough years on the job: when something suddenly became personal, the first response should not be excitement. It should be verification.
The signature was hurried. The M ended in a long trailing stroke, and the last two letters of Bell nearly ran together. Nora opened the photo library on her phone and searched Mom.

She had almost no photographs of her mother as an adult. Only a few old family pictures her grandmother had kept, plus photocopies of documents Nora had found years earlier in a bank safe-deposit box.
She found an old rental agreement.
Then she put the phone down.
Level B2 suddenly seemed very quiet.
Somewhere in the distance a document scanner gave a short mechanical chirp.
Her mother could not have signed for a document on that date.
Nora had been five when Mara Bell left Rivermere.

The family had told the same version of the story for years. On the evening of November 19, Mara had dropped Nora at her grandmother's house and said she had some work to finish. She never came back the next day. She had packed luggage, bought train tickets, and called her mother before seven to say she might have to leave the city for a while.
Later, someone claimed to have seen her in Edmonton.
Later still, there was a story about a postcard mailed from Vancouver.
A twenty-seven-year-old single mother had left a city while her life was in disorder. That was not illegal. Over time, the family had turned it into something no longer discussed.
When Nora was seven, she had asked, Why didn't Mom want me?
Her grandmother had said, Some people don't leave because they don't want you. They leave because they don't know how to stay.
By twelve, Nora had stopped asking.
At thirty-three, she had convinced herself she no longer cared about the answer.
Now an archival register from twenty-eight years earlier was telling her that on November 20, 1998, Mara Bell had still been in Rivermere.
She stared at those two words, then raised her hand.
An archivist noticed from across the room and came over. She was in her fifties, with short grey hair. Her badge read:
"This register." Nora pointed to the entry. "Could the date have been entered a day late?"
"Could someone have signed on another person's behalf?"
Elise did not answer immediately. She pushed her glasses higher on her nose.
"Ordinary people don't ask four questions in a row."
Elise returned her attention to the register.

"This wasn't an identity-verification system. Staff wrote down the name they were given, or the name they recognized. Someone picking something up for a colleague might not have left any formal authorization."
"So this doesn't prove the signer was Mara Bell."
That was the kind of answer she liked.
Not yes. Not no. A boundary.
She was about to close the register when Elise reached out.
Her fingers stopped a few millimetres above the paper.
"The date and the signature." Elise pointed without touching. "The register entry is blue-black. The signature is greyer. Not conclusive, but likely two pens."
"The date may have been entered by staff. The recipient may have signed separately."
Nora picked up her phone again.
Nora smiled. "A reporter's facial expression has no evidentiary value."
As Nora slid the register back, she noticed a faint pencil note at the bottom of the page. Not part of the formal entry. More like an internal staff comment.
"That staff couldn't reach the original recipient, so a returned copy was handled by someone else."
"So someone signed in person as M. Bell on November twentieth. Three days later, that person couldn't be reached."
For the first time, Elise's expression changed.
So slightly that someone who did not make a living watching people might have missed it. It was not surprise. It was more like the sensation of stepping down a staircase and finding one step missing.
"What did you just say?" Elise asked.
"The person whose name is on that line is my mother."
Elise looked at her for a full two seconds.
When she left Level B2, it was 5:12 p.m.
Just before the elevator doors closed, she looked back.
Elise was still standing beside the table.
zh: 里弗米尔市档案馆地下二层没有窗。
诺拉·贝尔不喜欢没有窗的地方。
不是因为幽闭，而是因为没有窗的房间很难判断时间。下午四点和晚上九点没有区别，十二月和六月没有区别。天花板上的白色灯管永远保持同一种亮度，空调从通风口送出经过过滤的冷空气，旧纸张、金属柜和灰尘混合成一种近乎无菌的气味。
这种地方让过去显得比现在更可靠。
诺拉对此一向保持怀疑。
她把第三只档案盒推到一旁，看了一眼笔记本电脑右上角。
她已经在这里坐了三个小时二十一分钟。
没有找到她真正想找的东西。
这本来只是一篇关于Alder Yard重建项目的报道。里弗米尔市议会两个月前批准了一项价值二十七亿加元的东区更新计划，要把废弃了几十年的铁路仓储区、旧化工厂和沿河工业用地改造成住宅、商业和公共绿地。
阳光。自行车。孩子。咖啡馆。一排排玻璃阳台面向河岸。没有人会从那些效果图里看出来，三十年前，那片土地曾被地下储油罐、溶剂和重金属污染得连野草都长得稀疏。
是什么时候开始，不能住人的土地变成了可以卖每平方英尺八百多加元的河景公寓？
这种问题通常不需要死人。
她翻开一份1998年的土地风险评估登记册。绿色硬壳封面，边角已经磨白。扫描部门尚未来得及处理这一批材料，所以她只能戴着档案馆发的薄棉手套，一页一页翻。
第三页开始是大量她已经看得麻木的公司名称。Halden Urban Group。Prairie Remediation Services。
公司破产，公司改名，公司被收购，董事死亡，律师退休。二十八年足够把一条责任链变成一片废墟。诺拉把手机放到书页旁，拍下一行数字。
不是因为地块。而是因为下面那一栏。Document received by: M. Bell
诺拉盯着那个名字看了两秒。
她没有马上做任何动作。
记者做久了，会养成一种习惯：当某件东西突然具有私人意义时，第一反应不应该是兴奋，而应该确认它是不是巧合。
她把登记册往自己面前拉近一点。
签名很潦草。M后面拖出一道很长的线，Bell最后两个字母几乎挤在一起。她把手机相册打开，搜索“Mom”。
她没有母亲成年后的生活照，只有外婆留下的一些旧照片，以及几年前她从银行保险箱里找到的几张文件复印件。
她翻到一张旧租赁合同。
地下二层忽然变得非常安静。
远处文件扫描机发出一声短促的机械鸣响。
她把那页纸重新看了一遍。
她母亲不可能在这一天签收文件。
诺拉五岁那年，母亲离开里弗米尔。
家里对这件事情有一套多年没有改变过的说法。十一月十九日晚上，玛拉把她送到外婆家，说有一些工作必须处理。第二天，她没有回来。但她留下了行李，买了火车票，还给母亲打过电话，说可能会离开城市一阵。
后来有人在埃德蒙顿见过她。
再后来，据说有人收到过从温哥华寄来的明信片。
一个二十七岁的单身母亲，在生活混乱的时候离开了一座城市。这种事情并不违反任何法律。随着年月过去，家里最终把它变成一个不再讨论的问题。诺拉七岁的时候问过：“妈妈为什么不要我？”外婆说：“有些人不是不要你，他们只是不知道怎么留下来。”
十二岁的时候她不再问了。
三十三岁的时候，她甚至已经认为自己不在乎答案。但现在，一个二十八年前的档案登记簿告诉她：1998年11月20日，她母亲还在里弗米尔。
诺拉把椅子往后推了一点。
她没有立刻给任何人打电话，而是继续检查。
移交单位：Mercer & Pike Legal。接收单位：Halden Urban Group。文件类别：Environmental Liability Addendum。
她盯着最后两个单词，然后举起手。
档案管理员从远处看见她，走了过来。那是一个五十多岁的女人，短灰发，胸牌上写着：ELISE WARDARCHIVAL CONSERVATION
“这份登记册。”诺拉指着那一行，“有没有可能登记日期晚了一天？”
伊莉丝低头看了一会儿。
她把眼镜往上推了一下。
“普通人不会连续问四个问题。”
诺拉笑了一下。“《里弗米尔纪事报》。”
伊莉丝重新看向登记册。
“这种旧登记系统不是身份证系统。工作人员认识谁，就直接写名字。有人替同事拿文件，也未必会留下正式授权。”
“所以这不能证明签名人就是Mara Bell。”
伊莉丝看了她一眼。“也不能。”
不是肯定，不是否定，只是边界。她正准备合上登记册，伊莉丝忽然伸手。
她的指尖没有碰纸，只停在距离页面几毫米的位置。
“登记项目是蓝黑墨水，签名偏灰。不是绝对，但很可能是两支笔。”
“意味着日期可能由工作人员填写，签名由领取人自己签。”
诺拉重新把手机拿起来。
诺拉笑了笑。“记者的表情不具有证据效力。”
诺拉把登记册推回去时，忽然看见页面最下方还有一行铅笔小字。不是正式登记。
更像工作人员留下的内部备注。
“通常表示联系不上原签收人，退回副本由别人处理。”
“所以十一月二十日有人以M. Bell的身份亲自签收。三天以后，这个人联系不上了。”
伊莉丝的表情第一次变了。
小到如果诺拉不是靠观察别人吃饭，也许根本不会注意。不是惊讶。更像是一个人在走楼梯时，脚下突然少了一阶。
伊莉丝看着她，足足两秒。
她离开地下二层时，已经五点十二分。
电梯门关上之前，她最后看了一眼。
伊莉丝还站在那张桌旁。
